draft.title: Misleading advertising
card: The Australian Consumer Law (ACL) bans businesses from making false or misleading claims in ads. A claim can mislead by what it says, or by what it leaves out.
False claim
a statement that is not true, such as saying a jacket is waterproof when it leaks, or that a product has won an award it has not won.
Bait advertising
advertising a product at a low price without enough stock to meet likely demand. The aim is to bring customers in, then sell them something else.
Hidden conditions
a catch that changes the offer but is not made clear, such as tiny print that adds fees to a "free" deal. The main message must not be cancelled out by the fine print.
draft.remember: The ACL bans ads that mislead: false claims, bait advertising and hidden conditions.

a.q: A shop advertises a TV at a very low price, but has only one in stock and tells shoppers it has sold out. Which type of banned advertising is this most likely to be?
opts: Bait advertising
A false claim about an award
A hidden condition in fine print
A normal sales promotion
a.why: The low price drew shoppers in, but the shop did not have enough stock to meet likely demand. That is bait advertising. A hidden condition would be a catch left out of the ad, which is not the problem here.
a.clue: Think about the price that brought people in and the stock available.

b.q: Kai's gym advertises "Join for $1 a week!" in large print. Tiny print at the bottom says a $300 joining fee applies. Why is this likely to break the Australian Consumer Law?
opts: A condition that changes the offer is hidden in small print
The gym did not have enough memberships for demand
The gym claimed an award that it has not won
Gyms are not allowed to advertise a weekly price
b.why: The large print suggests a cheap deal, but a major cost is buried in tiny print. That is a hidden condition that can mislead. It is not bait advertising, because nothing suggests the gym ran out of memberships.
b.clue: Look at where the $300 fee appears in the ad.

b.best: A condition that changes the offer is hidden in small print

problems.detail: Why (a) describes a hidden condition as 'a catch left out of the ad'. The card defines it as a catch that is in the ad but not made clear, such as tiny print. The why should match the card's wording.
